topic_title: Database Management Systems (DBMS): Foundations & Visual Intuition
overview: In 15 minutes, Maya guides you through the core ideas of DBMS using vivid visual analogies, from data storage basics to query processing, ending with a quick hands‑on demo and a synthesis activity.

modules.title: Data Foundations & Structure
modules.description: Visualizing how data is organized and stored.

steps.title: What is a DBMS? The Library Analogy
steps.concept_summary: Imagine a DBMS as a smart librarian who catalogs, stores, and retrieves books (data) efficiently.
steps.teacher_script: Hello! Today we're diving into the heart of any modern application: the Database Management System, or DBMS. Imagine walking into a massive library where every book, magazine, and manuscript is perfectly organized. The DBMS is the smart librarian who not only knows exactly where each item lives but also checks it out, returns it, and keeps track of who borrowed what—all in a split second. Just as the librarian shields you from the chaos of endless shelves, the DBMS hides the complex details of how data is stored on disks, letting you focus on asking questions like “Which customers bought product X last month?” Instead of rummaging through piles, you simply issue a query, and the librarian—our DBMS—fetches the answer instantly. This abstraction gives us consistency, security, and speed. Throughout this module, we'll explore how that librarian works behind the scenes, from cataloging (metadata) to indexing (quick look‑ups) and transaction management (making sure every operation is safe). Ready to meet your digital librarian? Let’s get started!

formative_question.prompt: If you think of a DBMS as a librarian, which of the following library tasks corresponds to the DBMS's 'query processor'?
options: Helping a patron find a specific book
Keeping a record of overdue books
formative_question.correct_answer: Helping a patron find a specific book
hints: The query processor interprets user requests
It translates a question into actions to locate data
common_misconceptions: Confusing query processing with data storage
Thinking the DBMS only stores data without handling requests

steps.title: Tables, Rows, and Columns: The Grid Blueprint
steps.concept_summary: Break down the relational model: tables are grids, rows are records, columns are attributes, like a spreadsheet of information.
steps.teacher_script: Hey there! Imagine you’re looking at a spreadsheet on your laptop – rows and columns neatly arranged, each cell holding a piece of data. In the world of databases, that very spreadsheet is called a table, and it’s the fundamental building block of the relational model. Each column represents an attribute – think of it as a property like "Student Name" or "Course ID" – while each row is a record, a single, complete entry that ties all those attributes together, like one student’s full profile. This grid layout lets us store massive amounts of structured information in a way that’s both human‑readable and machine‑efficient. As we dive deeper, you’ll see how primary keys uniquely identify rows, and how foreign keys link tables together, forming a powerful web of relationships. So, picture a library catalog: the table is the catalog, columns are the fields like title, author, and ISBN, and each row is a specific book. Ready to explore how this simple grid becomes the backbone of complex data systems?

visuals.title: Concept Visual
visuals.content: A relational table is like an Excel sheet: columns = attributes (e.g., Name, Age), rows = individual records (e.g., one person’s data).

visuals.title: Concept Visual
visuals.content:
graph LR
    Table[Table: Students]
    Column1[Column: StudentID]
    Column2[Column: Name]
    Column3[Column: Major]
    Row1[Row: (101, "Alice", "CS")]
    Row2[Row: (102, "Bob", "EE")]
    Table --> Column1
    Table --> Column2
    Table --> Column3
    Table --> Row1
    Table --> Row2

visuals.title: Concept Visual
Concept Visual
visuals.content:
- A table = a grid of rows (records) and columns (attributes).
- Columns define the data type and meaning of each field.
- Each row uniquely represents one entity, identified by a primary key.

formative_question.prompt: If you look at a table of employee data, which part of the grid would you point to in order to find the employee's salary for a specific person?
formative_question.correct_answer: You would locate the column labeled 'Salary' and then move to the row that corresponds to that specific employee; the intersecting cell gives the salary.
hints: First, identify what a column represents in a table.
Then, think about how you locate a particular individual's information.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the column (attribute) with the entire row (record).
Assuming the salary is stored in a separate table without a clear relationship.

modules.title: Operations & Queries
modules.description: Seeing how we interact with the data.

steps.title: SQL as a Recipe: SELECT, FROM, WHERE
steps.concept_summary: Visualize a SQL query as a cooking recipe where SELECT picks ingredients, FROM chooses the pantry, and WHERE applies filters.

steps.title: Live Query Walkthrough
steps.concept_summary: Maya runs a quick demo: creating a table, inserting rows, and retrieving specific records, reinforcing the recipe analogy.

modules.title: Integrity, Transactions & Reflection
modules.description: Ensuring data reliability and consolidating learning.

steps.title: Quick Quiz: Spot the Anomaly
steps.concept_summary: A visual multiple‑choice snapshot asks you to identify violations of primary key or foreign key rules.

steps.title: Design Your Mini‑DB
steps.concept_summary: You sketch a tiny database schema for a personal movie collection, applying tables, keys, and a simple SELECT query.
